title: The Water Cycle
summary: How the sun moves Earth's water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, and why the water cycle matters in a dry country like Saudi Arabia.
poll: Saving water is important even in a country that can make fresh water from the sea.

versions.title: Where Rain Comes From
versions.text:
It is a hot day. Get a cold glass of juice. Wait. Drops form on the glass. Where did they come from? The air!

Water moves all the time. It goes up to the sky. Then it falls. Then it goes up. This is the water cycle.

The sun heats the sea. Some of it turns to a gas. The gas is water vapor. You can not see it. We call this step evaporation.

The vapor goes up high. It is cold up there. It cools. It turns back to drops. We call this step condensation. The drops make a cloud. Look up. You can see it!

The drops bump. They join. They get big and fat. Then they fall. They fall as rain, snow, or hail. We call this step precipitation.

The rain lands. It runs to seas and lakes. Some sinks in the ground. The sun heats it. Up it goes. The cycle starts once more.

Saudi Arabia does not get much rain. But it still gets some. Dew forms on cool nights. Wells pull it up from deep in the ground. Big plants sit by the sea. They take the salt out of sea water. That is desalination.

versions.title: Where Rain Comes From
versions.text:
Pour a cold glass of juice on a hot day. Then wait a few minutes. Soon, small drops cover the glass. Where did they come from? They came from the air!

Water on Earth is always on the move. It goes up to the sky. It falls back down. Then it goes up again. This trip never ends. It is called the water cycle.

The sun heats the water in seas and lakes. Some of the water turns into a gas. The gas is called water vapor. You can not see it. This step is called evaporation.

The warm vapor floats up. High in the sky, the air is cold. The vapor cools and turns back into tiny drops of water. This step is called condensation. Lots of tiny drops make a cloud.

In the cloud, the drops bump and join. They grow big and heavy. Then they fall as rain, snow, or hail. This step is called precipitation.

The water lands on the ground. Some of it flows to rivers, lakes, and the sea. Some soaks into the ground. Then the sun heats the water once more, and the cycle goes on.

Saudi Arabia is a dry land. It does not get much rain. Still, people find water. On cool nights, dew forms on plants and cars. Wells pump up water from deep in the ground. Big plants by the sea take the salt out of sea water. This is called desalination.

versions.title: The Water Cycle
versions.text:
Pour a cold glass of juice. Do it on a hot day. Then wait a few minutes. Soon, tiny drops cover the outside of the glass. Nobody spilled a thing. The water came from the air around the glass!

Water on Earth is always on the move. It rises into the sky. It falls back to the ground. Then it rises again. This trip never ends. It is called the water cycle.

The cycle runs on heat from the sun. The sun warms seas, lakes, and rivers. Some of the water turns into a gas. You can not see it. This gas is called water vapor. The step is called evaporation.

The warm vapor floats up into the sky. High above the ground, the air is much colder. The vapor cools. It turns back into tiny drops of water. This step is called condensation. Millions of these drops make a cloud.

In a cloud, the little drops bump and join. When they get too heavy to float, they fall to Earth as rain, snow, or hail. This step is called precipitation.

Next, the water is collected. Some flows into rivers, lakes, and the sea. Some soaks into the soil and moves deep under the ground. Later, the sun warms the water again. The cycle starts over.

Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry land. Rain does not fall much. Still, people find water in smart ways. On cool nights, dew forms on plants and cars. Wells pump water up from deep in the ground. Large plants near the sea take the salt out of sea water. Then people can drink it. This is called desalination.

The water you drink today may once have been part of a cloud!

versions.title: The Water Cycle
versions.text:
Pour a cold glass of juice on a hot afternoon and wait a few minutes. Soon, tiny drops of water cover the outside of the glass. Nobody spilled anything. The water came from the air around the glass, and it shows one small part of a great journey.

Water on Earth is always on the move. It rises into the sky, falls back to the ground, and then rises again. Because this journey never ends, scientists call it the water cycle.

The sun powers the whole cycle. Its heat warms seas, lakes, and rivers. As the water warms, some of it changes into a gas that you can not see. This gas is called water vapor, and this step is called evaporation.

The warm vapor drifts up into the sky. High above the ground, the air is much colder. As the vapor cools, it changes back into tiny drops of water. This step is called condensation. When millions of these drops gather, they form a cloud.

Inside a cloud, the tiny drops bump into each other and join. When the drops get too heavy to float, they fall to Earth as rain, snow, or hail. This step is called precipitation.

The last step is collection. Some of the water flows into rivers, lakes, and the sea. Some soaks into the soil and moves slowly deep under the ground. Later, the sun warms the water again, and the cycle begins once more.

Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry land. In many places, rain falls only a few times a year. Still, people there find water in clever ways. On cool nights, dew forms on plants, rocks, and cars. Wells pump water from deep under the ground. Large plants along the coast take the salt out of sea water so people can drink it. This process is called desalination.

So the next time you drink a glass of water, remember that it may once have floated in a cloud!

versions.title: The Water Cycle: Earth's Endless Journey
versions.text:
Pour a glass of cold juice on a hot afternoon and wait a few minutes. Soon, tiny beads of water cover the outside of the glass. Nobody spilled a drop. The water came from the air around the glass. It shows one small part of a journey that never stops.

Water on Earth is always moving. It rises into the sky, falls back to the ground, and then rises again. Scientists call this endless journey the water cycle.

The sun powers the whole cycle. Its heat warms oceans, lakes, and rivers. As the water warms, some of it changes into a gas you cannot see. It is called water vapor. This step is called evaporation. When seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind in the ocean. So the vapor is fresh water.

Warm air carries the vapor high into the sky. Up there, the air is much colder. As the vapor cools, it condenses, which means it changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water. Each droplet forms around a speck of dust. Millions of droplets together make a cloud.

Inside a cloud, the droplets crash into each other and join. When they grow too heavy to float, they fall to Earth as rain, snow, or hail. This step is called precipitation.

Next comes collection. Some water runs across the land into rivers, lakes, and oceans. Some seeps into the soil and slowly trickles down to become groundwater. Then the sun warms the water again, and the cycle repeats.

The water cycle matters a great deal in Saudi Arabia. Rain is rare there. When a heavy storm does arrive, dry valleys called wadis can suddenly fill with rushing water. On cool desert nights, vapor condenses into dew on plants and rocks. Much of the country's water is groundwater that collected long ago, and it refills very slowly. To make more fresh water, large desalination plants along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf remove salt from seawater.

The water you drink today may once have floated in a cloud over a faraway sea.

Pour a glass of chilled juice on a scorching afternoon and wait a few minutes. Before long, tiny beads of water cover the outside of the glass, even though nobody spilled a drop. The moisture originated in the surrounding air, and it demonstrates one modest part of a remarkable journey that has been continuing for billions of years.

Water on Earth is constantly in motion, rising into the atmosphere, returning to the ground, and then rising once again. Scientists describe this continuous journey as the water cycle, and because the cycle recycles the same water, the total amount on our planet stays almost the same.

The sun supplies the energy that drives the entire cycle. Its heat warms oceans, lakes, and rivers, causing some of the water to transform into an invisible gas called water vapor, a process known as evaporation. Plants contribute as well, releasing vapor through tiny openings in their leaves in a process called transpiration. When seawater evaporates, the dissolved salt remains behind in the ocean, which is why the rising vapor is fresh water.

Ascending air currents carry the vapor high into the atmosphere, where temperatures are considerably lower. As the vapor cools, condensation occurs: the gas changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water, each forming around a microscopic particle of dust or salt. When billions of droplets accumulate, they become a visible cloud.

Within a cloud, droplets collide and combine into progressively larger drops. Once they become too heavy to remain suspended, gravity pulls them to Earth as rain, snow, or hail, a stage called precipitation.

The final stage is collection. Some water flows across the land into rivers, lakes, and oceans, while some seeps into the soil and gradually trickles downward to replenish groundwater. Layers of rock and sand that hold this underground water are called aquifers.

The water cycle is particularly significant in Saudi Arabia, where rainfall is scarce and unpredictable. When a powerful storm does arrive, dry valleys called wadis can suddenly fill with rushing water. On cool desert nights, vapor condenses into dew on vegetation and rocks. Much of the country's water comes from aquifers that filled thousands of years ago, when the climate was wetter, and they replenish extremely slowly. To produce additional fresh water, enormous desalination plants along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf remove salt from seawater. Some plants heat seawater and then cool the vapor, imitating the natural cycle, but desalination requires a great deal of energy.

The water in your glass today may once have drifted in a cloud above a distant ocean.

versions.text:
If you pour a glass of chilled juice on a scorching afternoon and wait several minutes, then before long minuscule beads of moisture accumulate on the exterior of the glass, even though nobody spilled a single drop. The moisture originated in the surrounding atmosphere, and it demonstrates one modest component of an extraordinary planetary journey that has been continuing, essentially uninterrupted, for billions of years.

Water on Earth is perpetually in motion, ascending into the atmosphere, returning to the surface, and subsequently ascending once again. Scientists characterize this continuous circulation as the water cycle, and because the cycle recirculates the identical water repeatedly, the total quantity on our planet remains essentially constant across enormous spans of geological time.

The sun supplies the energy that ultimately drives the entire cycle. Its radiation warms oceans, lakes, and rivers, causing a portion of the water to transform into an invisible gas called water vapor, a process known as evaporation. Vegetation contributes significantly as well, releasing vapor through microscopic openings in its leaves in a process called transpiration. When seawater evaporates, the dissolved salt remains behind in the ocean, which explains why the ascending vapor is fresh water rather than salty.

Rising air currents transport the vapor high into the atmosphere, where temperatures are considerably lower. As the vapor cools, condensation occurs: the gas reverts to minuscule droplets of liquid water, each of which forms around a microscopic particle of dust, salt, or smoke. When billions of these droplets accumulate, they become a visible cloud.

Within a cloud, droplets collide and coalesce into progressively larger drops, and once they become too heavy to remain suspended, gravity pulls them toward the surface as rain, snow, or hail, a stage collectively called precipitation.

During the concluding stage, known as collection, some water flows across the landscape into rivers, lakes, and oceans, while some infiltrates the soil and gradually percolates downward to replenish groundwater. Subterranean layers of porous rock and sediment that store this water are called aquifers.

When an intense storm does arrive, normally arid valleys called wadis can abruptly fill with torrential, dangerous floodwater, whereas on cool desert nights atmospheric vapor condenses into dew on vegetation and rocks. Much of the country's water originates in aquifers that accumulated thousands of years ago, during a considerably wetter climatic period, and they replenish extraordinarily slowly, which makes conservation essential. To generate additional fresh water, enormous desalination facilities along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf extract salt from seawater. Certain facilities heat seawater and subsequently cool the resulting vapor, deliberately imitating the natural cycle, although desalination consumes a substantial amount of energy.

keyWords.definition: a set of steps that happen again and again in the same order
keyWords.example: Day turns into night and back into day in a cycle.

keyWords.definition: water that has turned into a gas you cannot see
keyWords.example: Steam from the hot soup turned into vapor and disappeared.

keyWords.definition: when liquid water is heated and turns into a gas
keyWords.example: After the rain stopped, evaporation dried the puddles in the school yard.

keyWords.definition: when a gas cools and turns back into drops of liquid
keyWords.example: Condensation made the car window wet on the cool morning.

keyWords.definition: water that falls from clouds, such as rain, snow, or hail
keyWords.example: The weather report said there would be no precipitation this week.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to keep a glass of juice cold
How water moves from Earth to the sky and back again
Why it never rains in Saudi Arabia
How people build wells in the desert
questions.why: The whole article explains the steps water takes as it goes up into the sky and comes back down, over and over.

wrong.A: The cold glass is only used at the start to catch the reader's interest.
wrong.C: The article says rain is rare in Saudi Arabia, not that it never rains.
wrong.D: Wells are mentioned in one sentence, but they are not the main topic.

questions.stem: What gives water the heat it needs to evaporate?
options: The wind
The clouds
The sun
The ground
questions.why: The article says the sun warms the sea, and some of the water turns into a gas.

wrong.A: The article does not say wind heats the water.
wrong.B: Clouds form later, after the vapor cools.
wrong.D: Water soaks into the ground at the end of the cycle; the ground does not heat it.

questions.stem: What are clouds made of?
options: Tiny drops of water
Smoke from the sea
Salt and sand
Water vapor that is hot
questions.why: The article says the cooled vapor turns into tiny drops, and the drops make clouds.

wrong.B: The article never says clouds are made of smoke.
wrong.C: Salt stays in the sea; clouds are made of water drops.
wrong.D: Vapor must cool and turn into drops before a cloud forms.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "They fall as rain, snow, or hail. This step is precipitation." What does precipitation mean?
options: Water that soaks into the ground
Water that turns into a gas
Salt that is taken out of the sea
Water that falls from the sky
questions.why: Rain, snow, and hail all fall from clouds, so precipitation means water falling from the sky.

wrong.A: That describes collection, the step after precipitation.

questions.stem: What happens right after water vapor rises and cools?
options: It turns into salt.
It turns back into tiny drops.
It sinks into the ground.
It falls as hail right away.
questions.why: The article says that when the vapor cools high in the sky, it turns back into tiny drops. This is condensation.

wrong.A: Salt does not come from vapor; salt stays in the sea.
wrong.C: Water sinks into the ground after it falls, much later in the cycle.
wrong.D: The drops must first join and get heavy before anything falls.

questions.stem: Why do drops form on the outside of a cold glass of juice?
options: The juice leaks through the glass.
Someone splashed water on it.
Vapor in the air cools and turns into drops.
The sun heats the glass.
questions.why: The article says the drops came from the air. Cold makes vapor turn back into drops, just like condensation in the sky.

wrong.A: The article says nobody spilled anything; the water came from the air.
wrong.B: The article says the water came from the air, not from a splash.
wrong.D: Heat from the sun causes evaporation, not drops on a cold glass.

questions.stem: Why does Saudi Arabia need to take the salt out of sea water?
options: The country gets very little rain.
Sea water is much too cold for people to drink.
People want to sell the salt.
There is no sea near the country.
questions.why: Because rain is rare, people must find other ways to get fresh water, such as removing salt from sea water.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about the temperature of sea water.
wrong.C: The article does not say anything about selling salt.
wrong.D: The article says the plants that clean sea water are by the sea, so there is sea nearby.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By comparing rain in two countries
By telling a story about one raindrop's family
By listing the problems of a dry country and then their answers
By explaining the steps of the water cycle in order
questions.why: The author explains evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation, then collection, in the order they happen.

wrong.A: Only Saudi Arabia is described; no two countries are compared.
wrong.B: The article gives facts, not a made-up story about a family.
wrong.C: The article mostly explains steps; only the last part talks about finding water.

LOW.prompt: Explain the water cycle in your own words. Name at least three of its steps and tell what happens in each one.
checklist: I named at least three steps of the water cycle.
I told what happens to the water in each step.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: The water cycle has many steps. First, the sun heats water and evaporation turns it into vapor. Next, the vapor rises and cools, and condensation changes it into tiny drops that form clouds. Then the drops get heavy and fall as rain or snow, and this is called precipitation. This cycle keeps happening again and again.

keyWords.definition: water in the form of a gas that you cannot see
keyWords.example: On a humid day, the air is full of water vapor.

keyWords.definition: to change from a gas into a liquid when cooled
keyWords.example: Steam from the kettle will condense into drops on the cold kitchen tiles.

keyWords.definition: rain, snow, or hail that falls from clouds to the ground
keyWords.example: The mountains of Asir usually get more precipitation than the central desert.

keyWords.definition: water that is stored under the ground in soil and rock
keyWords.example: The farmer dug a well to reach the groundwater below his field.

keyWords.definition: the process of removing salt from seawater so people can use it
keyWords.example: Thanks to desalination, the coastal city has enough water for its homes.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Water moves in an endless cycle that is powered by the sun and matters to every place on Earth.
Clouds form only over the oceans and never over deserts.
Desalination is the only way that people in Saudi Arabia can get the fresh water they need.
Rain is more important than snow or hail.
questions.why: The article explains each stage of the water cycle, shows that the sun drives it, and explains why it matters in Saudi Arabia.

wrong.B: The article does not say where clouds can or cannot form.
wrong.C: The article also names groundwater, rain, and dew as water sources.
wrong.D: The article treats rain, snow, and hail as types of precipitation without ranking them.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does each cloud droplet form around?
options: A grain of salt from a wadi
A drop of seawater
A speck of dust
A tiny ice crystal
questions.why: The article says each droplet forms around a tiny speck or particle of dust.

wrong.A: Wadis are dry valleys on land and are not part of how droplets form.
wrong.B: Seawater stays in the ocean; only fresh vapor rises.
wrong.D: Ice crystals are not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: According to the article, where are Saudi Arabia's large desalination plants?
options: Inside dry wadis
Along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf
Next to mountain lakes
In the middle of the desert, far from the coast
questions.why: The article says the desalination plants are along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, where there is seawater.

wrong.A: Wadis are dry valleys that flood only after storms.
wrong.C: The article does not mention mountain lakes.
wrong.D: The plants need seawater, so they are on the coast, not deep inland.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "Some seeps into the soil and slowly trickles down to become groundwater." What does seeps mean?
options: Flows slowly through small spaces
Freezes into hard ice
Rises quickly into the warm air above it
Splashes loudly over rocks
questions.why: Water that moves slowly into soil passes through tiny spaces, which is what seeps means.

wrong.B: Nothing in the sentence describes freezing.
wrong.C: The water moves down into the soil, not up into the air.
wrong.D: The sentence says the water moves slowly, not loudly or quickly.

questions.stem: Why is the rain that falls from clouds fresh water, even though much of it starts in the salty ocean?
options: Clouds filter out the salt as they move.
Rain mixes with river water as it falls.
Desalination plants clean the clouds.
The salt stays behind when seawater evaporates.
questions.why: The article explains that when seawater evaporates, the salt stays in the ocean, so the vapor is fresh.

wrong.A: The salt never reaches the clouds, so there is nothing to filter.
wrong.B: Rain is already fresh before it reaches any river.
wrong.C: Desalination plants treat seawater on land, not clouds.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why should people in Saudi Arabia use groundwater carefully?
options: Groundwater is always too salty to drink.
It refills very slowly, so it can run low.
Pumping water from wells makes the dry wadis flood.
Groundwater turns into dew at night.
questions.why: The article says much of the groundwater collected long ago and refills very slowly, so using too much could use it up.

wrong.A: The article says groundwater is part of the country's water supply, so it is usable.
wrong.C: Wadis flood because of heavy storms, not because of wells.
wrong.D: Dew forms from vapor in the air, not from groundwater.

questions.stem: How are dew on a desert plant and a cloud in the sky alike?
options: Both are made of salt.
Both form when the sun heats the ground during the day.
Both form when water vapor cools and condenses.
Both are kinds of precipitation.
questions.why: The article says vapor condenses into droplets to make clouds, and vapor condenses into dew on cool nights.

wrong.A: Neither one is made of salt; both are fresh water.
wrong.B: Heat causes evaporation; both dew and clouds need cooling.
wrong.D: Dew does not fall from clouds, so it is not precipitation.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the section about Saudi Arabia?
options: To show how the water cycle matters in a dry country
To prove that Saudi Arabia has more rain than most other countries in the world
To teach readers how to build a desalination plant
To describe the history of wells in Arabia
questions.why: The section connects the science of the water cycle to the reader's own dry country and its water sources.

wrong.B: The article says rain is rare in Saudi Arabia.
wrong.C: The article mentions desalination plants but does not explain how to build one.
wrong.D: The article does not give a history of wells.

MID.prompt: Saudi Arabia gets very little rain. Explain how the country still gets the water it needs. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I used at least two details from the article.
I explained how each water source connects to the water cycle.
MID.modelAnswer: Even though Saudi Arabia gets very little rain, the country still finds the water it needs in a few ways. One detail is that much of the water underground, called groundwater, collected long ago and people can still use it today. Another detail is that desalination plants along the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf take salty seawater and remove the salt to make fresh water. Even dew forms on cool desert nights when vapor in the air condenses on plants and rocks. These sources connect to the water cycle because they all come from water that evaporated, condensed, or fell as precipitation at some point.

keyWords.definition: the change of a gas into a liquid as it cools
keyWords.example: Condensation dripped from the air conditioner onto the balcony below.

keyWords.definition: any form of water, such as rain, snow, or hail, that falls from clouds
keyWords.example: Scientists measured the precipitation in the region over ten years.

keyWords.definition: the release of water vapor from plants through small openings in their leaves
keyWords.example: On a hot day, transpiration from the trees made the garden air feel damp.

keyWords.definition: an underground layer of rock or sand that holds water
keyWords.example: Engineers drilled deep into the aquifer to supply the new farm.

keyWords.definition: the removal of salt from seawater to make fresh water
keyWords.example: The coastal city depends on desalination for most of its drinking water.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Desalination will soon replace the natural water cycle completely in every dry country on Earth.
Saudi Arabia's aquifers are the largest in the world.
Transpiration is the most important stage of the water cycle.
The sun-driven water cycle constantly recycles Earth's water, which is especially important in a dry land.
questions.why: The article explains how the cycle works and ends by showing why it is so important where rain is scarce.

wrong.A: The article presents desalination as an extra source, not a replacement for the cycle.
wrong.B: The article never compares the size of Saudi aquifers with others.
wrong.C: Transpiration is one detail; no stage is called the most important.

questions.stem: According to the article, how do plants add water vapor to the air?
options: By releasing it through tiny openings in their leaves
By pulling it up from deep aquifers and sending it straight into the clouds
By melting snow with their roots
By turning dew into rain
questions.why: The article describes transpiration: plants release vapor through microscopic openings in their leaves.

wrong.B: Plants do not move water directly into clouds from aquifers.
wrong.C: The article does not say roots melt snow.
wrong.D: Dew does not turn into rain; this is not in the article.

questions.stem: According to the article, when did many of Saudi Arabia's aquifers fill with water?
options: During last winter's storms
Thousands of years ago, when the climate was wetter
When the first desalination plants were built
Every night, when cool air makes dew form on rocks
questions.why: The article states that the aquifers filled thousands of years ago, during a wetter climatic period.

wrong.A: The article says aquifers refill very slowly, so one winter could not fill them.
wrong.C: Desalination plants produce water from the sea, not aquifer water.
wrong.D: Dew forms on plants and rocks; it does not fill aquifers each night.

questions.stem: The article says that Saudi Arabia's old aquifers replenish very slowly. What does replenish mean?
options: Become polluted
Dry up completely
Fill up again
Move to the surface
questions.why: The aquifers lose water when people use it and only slowly gain it back, so replenish means to fill up again.

wrong.A: The sentence is about the amount of water, not its quality.
wrong.B: Drying up is the opposite of replenishing.
wrong.D: The water soaks downward into aquifers; nothing says it moves upward.

questions.stem: What causes the drops in a cloud to fall to Earth as precipitation?
options: The sun's heat pushes them down.
Dust particles break apart.
Gravity pulls them once they become too heavy to stay suspended.
Rising air currents carry them up to colder heights, where they freeze.
questions.why: The article says droplets combine into larger drops, and once they are too heavy, gravity pulls them down.

wrong.A: The sun's heat causes evaporation, which moves water upward.
wrong.B: Dust particles help droplets form; they do not make them fall.
wrong.D: Rising air carries vapor up; it does not make drops fall.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might desalination be an expensive way to produce water?
options: It works only during rare storms.
It uses a great deal of energy.
It takes thousands of years.
It can be done only in wadis after heavy storms.
questions.why: The article says desalination consumes a large amount of energy, and energy costs money.

wrong.A: Desalination uses seawater, so it does not depend on storms.
wrong.C: Thousands of years describes how long aquifers took to fill.
wrong.D: The plants are on the coast, not in wadis.

questions.stem: How is the desalination method that heats seawater similar to the natural water cycle?
options: Both rely on plants to release vapor.
Both take place only on cool desert nights.
Both depend on tiny particles of dust to pull the salt out of the water.
Both use evaporation and condensation, leaving the salt behind.
questions.why: Like the sun evaporating seawater, the plant heats water to make vapor, then cools the vapor so it condenses into fresh water, leaving salt behind.

wrong.A: Transpiration is part of the natural cycle only, not desalination.
wrong.B: Desalination plants do not depend on the time of night.
wrong.C: Dust helps droplets form in clouds; it does not remove salt.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin the article with a glass of cold juice?
options: To connect an everyday experience to the science of condensation
To argue that people should drink less juice
To explain how juice is made
To compare the taste of juice with the taste of seawater
questions.why: The water drops on the glass show condensation, a familiar example that leads into the explanation of the cycle.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say desalination solves Saudi Arabia's water problem, so saving water is no longer important. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that desalination completely solves Saudi Arabia's water problem, so saving water still matters. Although desalination plants along the coasts can turn seawater into fresh water, this process requires enormous amounts of energy and cannot reach every region, especially towns located far from the coast that depend on an ancient aquifer that refills extremely slowly. In addition, natural precipitation and the condensation that forms dew are limited in this arid climate, so groundwater supplies are not easily replaced once they are used up. Because both desalinated water and natural groundwater are costly or slow to renew, I believe people should keep conserving water rather than assuming desalination alone will always be enough.
